entities.summary:
**Paragraph 1 — Identity & Significance**: Spiral galaxies, named for their sweeping spiral arms of younger stars, were first observed in the 19th century as a distinct class of galaxies. The Andromeda Galaxy, our closest major spiral galaxy neighbor, has been a focal point for astronomers since the 20th century. The Hubble Space Telescope has enabled a wealth of new observations and insights into spiral galaxies' structure and evolution.

**Paragraph 2 — What Happened**: The discovery of spiral galaxies has led to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution, with most galaxies now believed to have formed from the merger of smaller galaxies. Our own Milky Way is thought to have formed from the collision of several smaller galaxies. The study of spiral galaxies has also shed light on the formation and migration of stars within them.

**Paragraph 3 — Legacy & Consequence**: The study of spiral galaxies continues to inform our understanding of the universe, with many ongoing and future surveys and missions aimed at mapping the universe in unprecedented detail. The discovery of dark matter in spiral galaxies has also opened new avenues for research into its role in the universe.

**Paragraph 4**: With over 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, the diversity of spiral galaxies is vast and complex, each with its unique characteristics and evolutionary history.
